pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Dehydration, caused by lack of water in the body, can occur in cold orwarm weather, anytime a person is sweating profusely and/or notdrinking enough (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Avoid dehydration by drinking plenty of fluids andeating enough throughout the day to keep your body well-balanced (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: If youbecome weary or develop a headache or body aches, or if you becomeconfused, rest in the shade and sip water until the symptoms subside (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: If the freezing continues, the area will stiffen andbecome grayish-white in color (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): To treat the victim, thaw theaffected area only if there is no risk of refreezing (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Put cold fingers under the armpit and the warm palm of your hand on frostbitten nose, ears, or cheeks (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In a shelter, if possible, put cold feet on a companion's barebelly, or immerse the affected area in lukewarm water, nowarmer than 108 degrees (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If blisters develop, apply a large steriledressing (p. 28).

Step 3 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 3 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Dispose of webbing that shows any sign of damage or that has anunknown history (p. 49).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Core Field Standard: For tying together the ends of two ropes, the most reliable knotis the double fisherman's knot (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 2: It can also be used to secure the ends of a piece of cord to form a runner (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 3: Half of a doublefisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Loosely loop one rope end twice around the other, then thread the end of that rope through the loops (p. 53).
Step 2 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Carefully tighten the two parts of the knot, then slide them (p. 53).
Step 3 (Climbing Core Field Standard): If they don't fit together neatly, the knot is incorrectly tied (p. 53).
Step 4 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The knot is commonlytied with accessory cord by a climber to ascend a rope or to secure abelay system in order to release the belayer (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Harness, Helmet and Gloves: Using a harness that fits properly helpsmake climbing and rappelling safer, morecomfortable, and fun (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 2: Commercially made climbing harnesses usually require only thatyou put your legs through leg loops and then secure the waiststrap with a buckle (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 3: The leg loops of some harnesses can beadjusted; you should just be able to slip two fingers between theloop and your thigh (p. 57).

Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 4: If the harnesses available to you are notadjustable, you will need to choose one that fits your body snuglybut not tight enough to restrict circulation (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): A 30-foot length of nylon tubular webbing can be wrappedaround your body and tied in special ways to form a reliabletied harness for climbing (p. 57).
Step 2 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): Each tied harness must be tied exactly rightevery time to ensure your safety (p. 57).
